claims.text: In-situ aberration-corrected TEM equipped with a heating stage can reveal atomic-scale structural rearrangements in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles as temperature increases.
Heating AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will induce atomic diffusion.
Heating AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles may induce phase segregation.
Observing temperature-dependent atomic rearrangements can provide insight into the thermodynamic stability of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are well mixed at room temperature.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a nearly equiatomic composition.
Atomic rearrangements, diffusion, and phase segregation will occur both at nanoparticle interfaces and within the bulk.
Thermal energy induces diffusion and atomic rearrangement in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Thermally induced diffusion and rearrangement lead to local compositional gradients.
Local compositional gradients and possible phase segregation underpin changes in thermal stability.
Real-time TEM imaging will show discernible atomic rearrangements as temperature increases.
Real-time TEM imaging will show emerging compositional heterogeneities as temperature increases.
Spatial resolution and nanoparticle size distribution may limit the observations.
Prolonged TEM exposure may cause beam damage that limits interpretation.
The relationship between temperature and diffusion rate or phase-segregation threshold cannot be quantified without further experimental calibration.
